articles.title: Beginner Python Learner's Guide: Building a Small-Scale Videogame with Limited Experience and Resources
articles.excerpt: Introduction: Overcoming the Beginner's Hurdle You’ve learned Python basics—syntax, data structures, maybe even a few algorithms. But now, staring at the blank screen, the question looms: “Can I actua…
articles.body: Introduction: Overcoming the Beginner's Hurdle You’ve learned Python basics—syntax, data structures, maybe even a few algorithms. But now, staring at the blank screen, the question looms: “Can I actually build something?” The fear is real. It’s not just about code; it’s about translating abstract concepts into a functional, tangible project. Let’s break this down. First, the mechanism of self-doubt : Beginners often assume that “building” requires mastery. Wrong. The real risk isn’t your skill level—it’s overcomplicating the scope . A 200-line escape room game? Possible. But only if you decompose the problem into smaller, testable components. For example, player movement alone can be a 20-line module. Puzzle logic? Another 30 lines.
articles.author: Denis Lavrentyev

articles.title: Designing Android expense drafts from NotificationListenerService without bank login
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I build Money Tracker (Android: Money Tracker-Expense & Budget; iOS: Money Tracker:Expense & Budget). I write as daniel zheng. This is a product/engineering note about a privacy-constraine…
articles.body: Disclosure: I build Money Tracker (Android: Money Tracker-Expense & Budget; iOS: Money Tracker:Expense & Budget). I write as daniel zheng . This is a product/engineering note about a privacy-constrained draft pipeline — not a growth hack, not fake savings %, and not a claim of official bank partnerships. Most expense apps tip toward one of two extremes: (1) open banking / account sync, or (2) pure manual entry that users abandon after three days. Money Tracker sits on a third path: local capture → draft → user confirm → ledger . No bank password. No silent statement pull. On Android, one optional Premium path feeds that pipeline from NotificationListenerService : when another app posts a notification that looks like a payment, we propose a draft.

articles.title: Deduplicating 12,000 job postings taught me the same job is posted five times
articles.excerpt: I built a job search API that aggregates live postings by keyword and location, and the first version of the results was embarrassing: search "ML engineer Berlin" and you'd get the same role from the…
articles.body: I built a job search API that aggregates live postings by keyword and location, and the first version of the results was embarrassing: search "ML engineer Berlin" and you'd get the same role from the same company four or five times, because it was scraped onto four different boards. Agents consuming the API would waste context window on duplicates and look careless doing it. The fix was a fuzzy matching pass on (normalized title, normalized company, location) before returning results. Normalizing titles meant lowercasing, stripping punctuation, and collapsing things like "Sr." / "Senior" / "III" — because job boards can't agree on how to spell seniority either.

articles.title: ERP Module Integration Requirements Checklist
articles.excerpt: Modular enterprise resource planning systems often suffer from integration failures when independently developed modules make conflicting assumptions about data ownership, state transitions, and event…
articles.body: Modular enterprise resource planning systems often suffer from integration failures when independently developed modules make conflicting assumptions about data ownership, state transitions, and event ordering. A team might build a purchasing module and an inventory module that pass all local unit tests yet fail during integration because one service assumes it owns the authoritative stock quantity while the other modifies it concurrently. Quick solution: Establish a written interface contract and a data ownership table before writing code. Define the event schema, the authoritative source of truth, and failure behavior in a shared specification.

articles.title: AI Bot vs Chatbot: How to Choose
articles.excerpt: A regular bot is a program, often written in Python. An AI bot is a bot connected to a language model such as GPT, Claude, Gemini or Kimi. A regular bot performs functions defined in its code. An AI b…
articles.body: A regular bot is a program, often written in Python. An AI bot is a bot connected to a language model such as GPT, Claude, Gemini or Kimi. A regular bot performs functions defined in its code. An AI bot can handle different requests, act independently, retain memory and use connected tools I use both. When I need a strict sequence and a process that follows a plan, I use regular bots - programs written in Python. When I need flexibility and different ways to handle a task, I use AI bots When a regular bot is enough Say you need to retrieve data from a spreadsheet every day, calculate a total using the same formula and send it to Telegram. The sequence is known in advance.

articles.title: Stop Letting AI Agents Run Commands Blindly: Meet Zero-Trust Sandbox Auditor
articles.excerpt: Stop Letting AI Agents Run Commands Blindly: Meet Zero-Trust Sandbox Auditor Every developer I know is experimenting with autonomous AI coding agents—Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Devin, GitHub Copil…
articles.body: Stop Letting AI Agents Run Commands Blindly: Meet Zero-Trust Sandbox Auditor Every developer I know is experimenting with autonomous AI coding agents—Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Devin, GitHub Copilot Workspace, or custom agentic loops. We grant them terminal access, watch them plan tasks, write code, resolve issues, and install dependencies. It feels like magic. Until you ask yourself the uncomfortable question: What happens when an AI agent runs npm install or cargo build on a repository with an obfuscated postinstall hook or a malicious build script? Or worse: What if the agent has access to your unencrypted ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.aws/credentials ? What if the container it runs inside has /var/run/docker.sock mounted, allowing instant root escape to the host?

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force launched an experimental Super Strypi rail-launched rocket carrying 13 tiny satellites, but it failed just after liftoff from Hawaii.
articles.body: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms.

articles.excerpt: Researchers say group may have been Kremlin-sponsored in search of diplomatic targets.
articles.body: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.

articles.title: 'Trials and Tribble-ations' at 30: The classic 'Star Trek: Deep Space Nine' episode that brought Captains Kirk and Sisko face-to-face
articles.excerpt: How "Forrest Gump", pizza, and a massive supporting cast of furballs came together to make one of "Star Trek"'s finest hours.
articles.body: When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history , but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment. Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney).

articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA's Swift space telescope crashed back to Earth today (Nov. 4), three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost the observatory to a higher orbit.
articles.body: NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road. Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit. The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.
